definition: This is a comparison of frontier models in generative AI, according to aggregates of benchmarks..
details: This is a comparison of frontier models in generative AI, according to aggregates of benchmarks.

explainer.lead: A comparison of generative AI models combines benchmark results to show how frontier models perform relative to one another. It helps readers spot overall patterns, but a single summary can hide important differences between tasks.

tiers.eli5: Think of each model taking several school tests, such as answering questions or writing code. Combining the grades gives a quick report card, but two models with the same average may be good at very different subjects.
tiers.practitioner: Use benchmark aggregates to shortlist models, then inspect the task-level scores and evaluation settings that matter for the application. Check that models were tested under comparable conditions and avoid treating a small aggregate lead as proof of universal superiority.
tiers.paperLevel: For model m, an aggregate can be written A(m) = Agg_b s(m, b), where s(m, b) is its result on benchmark b and Agg is an aggregation rule such as a mean. Comparability depends on the selected benchmarks, scoring scales, weighting, and evaluation conditions; aggregation can also conceal weak performance on individual tasks.

explainer.example: Suppose one model scores 80 on reasoning and 60 on coding, while another scores 70 on both. Both have an unweighted mean of 70, yet the first is stronger on reasoning and weaker on coding.

explainer.intuition: Benchmark aggregates work like a combined report card: they compress many test results into a manageable comparison. The summary is useful only when the included tests and testing conditions suit the comparison being made.
howItWorks: Choose the frontier models to compare.
Evaluate them on a set of benchmarks.
Put the benchmark scores on comparable scales where needed.
Combine the scores using an aggregation rule.
Inspect both the aggregate and individual results.
explainer.whyItMatters: Aggregates make large benchmark tables easier to interpret and support quick model comparisons. Reading them alongside task-level results reduces the risk of choosing a model from a misleading overall ranking.
misconceptions: A higher aggregate does not mean a model is better at every task.
Aggregates from different benchmark sets are not automatically comparable.
Benchmark rankings do not guarantee equal performance in a particular application.
